title: Ten-day retreats
hook: hand in your phone, stop talking, sit: S. N. Goenka's silent ten-day courses

segments.voice: Yesterday: samatha, and a bowl of water left to settle. Your line was calm. Did five breaths at one spot come before an answer? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-one.

Hand in your phone at the door. Hand in your books and your notebook too. From this evening on, no talking to the other students. No texting, no gestures, not even catching someone's eye across the dining hall. Wake before dawn. Sit. Eat simply. Sit. Listen to a recorded talk in the evening. Sleep. Then do it again, for ten days. That's the shape of the silent courses taught by S. N. Goenka, a teacher who learned vipassana in Burma and carried it to India and far beyond. People sign up for this on purpose. Today is what happens inside those ten days.
screen: `HAND IN YOUR PHONE.` → `NO TALKING, NO GESTURES, NO EYE CONTACT.` → `TEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: The two days before this one were calm and insight, samatha and vipassana. Goenka's course is built to walk through both, in order. Here's the shape of it. First, the silence. It's called noble silence: silence of speech and of body, held among the students for nearly the whole course. A student can still speak with the teacher about practice, or with staff about practical needs. The point isn't punishment. Without talk, the mind has nowhere to hide, and the meditation gets the attention that conversation usually takes. Students also agree to keep basic moral precepts during the course, like not killing and not stealing. Tomorrow says more about those. Second, calm first. The early days are spent on the breath alone, watching it at a small area around the nose. It's yesterday's practice, narrowed and repeated until the mind steadies. Third, then insight. With the mind steadier, students are taught to move attention through the body, part by part, observing sensations and how they change, without craving the pleasant ones or pushing away the unpleasant ones. That's the day before yesterday's line, watch it change, practiced at length. Near the end, the silence lifts, and students are taught a practice of goodwill toward all beings. Fourth, how it's offered. In Goenka's tradition, the courses charge no fee. Food and lodging are covered by donations from students who've already finished a course and want others to have the chance. So the person beside you in silence has been carried there, in part, by strangers who sat before. Not everyone who hears about this wants to try it. Imagining it is a practice too, and that's today's.
screen: `NOBLE SILENCE: SPEECH AND BODY.` · `CALM FIRST: THE BREATH AT THE NOSE.` · `THEN INSIGHT: SENSATIONS, PART BY PART.` · `NO FEE: CARRIED BY PAST STUDENTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: imagine ten silent days. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then walk yourself through the first morning. The phone is gone. Nobody to talk to. A bell before dawn, a cushion, the breath at the nose. What comes up? Relief? Dread? Curiosity? A list of everyone who'd need to know where you were? Just notice what shows up, without deciding anything. Then come back to the breath at the nose for the rest of the time, as if this were the first sitting of day one. The bell holds the time.
Ten-day retreats. S. N. Goenka's silent vipassana courses: calm on the breath first, then insight into sensations, offered without a fee. Today's word.
Your line: ten silent days. Today, take a small slice of it: one meal or one walk with no phone and no talking, just the food or the steps. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Students on Goenka-style courses live at a center for ten days in noble silence, keep basic precepts, practice breath meditation and then vipassana body scanning for long stretches each day, and the courses run on donations from past students.

fork.setup: it's the third day of a ten-day course, and you badly want to tell the person next to you about a dream. what does noble silence ask?
options: keep it to yourself, and take it back to the cushion.
fork.reveal: noble silence covers speech and body: no talk, no gestures, no notes among students. the mind has nowhere to hide, and that's the point.

notes: Editor pass: cut the stock reassurance 'and that's fine'; varied the repeated 'four ways' teach frame; fixed a garbled review note.

Course details are general and paraphrased; confirm against the current code of discipline: noble silence among students (no speech, gestures, notes or eye contact), students may speak with the teacher and management; phones, books and writing materials handed in; precepts kept; early days anapana at the area around the nostrils; then vipassana body scanning; silence lifted near the end and metta taught; no fee, courses run on donations from students who have completed a course.

'a teacher who learned vipassana in Burma and carried it to India and far beyond': Goenka learned from Sayagyi U Ba Khin in Burma (Myanmar). 'Far beyond' paraphrases the index hook ('spread this practice worldwide'); no counts of centers or students are given under the claims rule.
'the first sitting of day one' and 'third day' in the fork are framing, not course-schedule claims; the exact day the switch to vipassana happens was left out.
'Not everyone who hears about this wants to try it' is a plain hedge.
Tomorrow (the monk's rule) teaches the five precepts; today mentions them only in passing.
